newsitem.title: FRANCE: France planning to restrict art exports - paper.
newsitem.headline: France planning to restrict art exports - paper.

text.p: France, fearing that many art works are disappearing abroad, is secretly preparing to crack down on exports in a move likely to cut the value of masterpieces in the country, the daily newspaper Liberation reported on Tuesday.
Auctioneers fear the threat of a new law could prompt collectors to pack up their most precious works and flee before any legislation takes effect.
Restrictions might also be unworkable with open European Union borders.
Liberation said the Ministry of Culture was planning to scrap a 1992 law that allows collectors to get compensation if the state declares a work a "national treasure" and refuses an export permit.
A painting sold in New York or Tokyo can fetch far more than works limited to France.

In the most spectacular case, owners of Vincent Van Gogh's "Jardin a Auvers," one of the Dutch artist's last masterpieces painted in 1890, won 145 million francs ($29m) from the French state under a court order when its export was banned.

Under the new draft, Liberation said the state could declare works national treasures and bar their export without paying a franc of compensation. The Culture Ministry declined immediate comment on the report.

"If the rumours are true, we're moving towards totalitarian methods," said Jacques Tajan, an auctioneer who tried to sell the Jardin a Auvers last month but failed when the top bid of 32 million francs ($6.4m) fell short of the reserve price.

Tajan told Reuters a French art collector visited him on Monday to ask advice about whether it was better to take his paintings out of the country, or at least apply for export permits under the existing legislation.
"I think I would in his position," Tajan said. "If they're banned from leaving the country they will lose two-thirds of their value."
But the current system has been widely criticised, especially because the payment over the Jardin a Auvers, still in a private collection, gutted France's budget for new acquisitions.

Pierre Rosenberg, the director of the Louvre museum, said the 1992 law was "disastrous" because it had barred exports without giving museums the cash to buy new works. "The French heritage is threatened as never before," he told Liberation.

He noted that Rubens' "Decapitation of St John the Baptist" and Poussin's "Agony in the Garden of Olives" both recently left France. Just 39 works have been denied export permits of 11,000 applications.
Tajan urged France to work out EU-wide legislation on art works and said France should ensure some system of compensation for works denied export permits.
He said restrictive laws did not work. "Italy is probably the most prohibitive country in Europe but people just smuggle works out. The law is so strict that no one asks for permits," he said.
